issues.title: SWAR first+last-byte candidate scan in FindStrInStr for short haystacks
issues.hypothesis: In q13 the orders TABLE_SCAN with the NOT LIKE '%w1%w2%' filter is 2.40s of about 3.35s total operator CPU. Microbenchmarks at 8 threads, as scan operator CPU on orders: two integer columns only 0.41s; plus decoding o_comment with length(o_comment)>45 1.92s; NOT contains(o_comment,'qqqqqqq') with a rare first byte 2.23s; NOT contains 'eeeeeee' with a common first byte 2.44s; the actual q13 NOT LIKE 2.36s. At 1 thread the same scan is 2.09s, so the cost is per-row compute, not bandwidth. Matching therefore costs about 0.3-0.5s CPU on top of decoding. Even with a first byte that never occurs it costs about 0.3s, which is the fixed cost per string of calling memchr. FindStrInStr (src/function/scalar/string/contains.cpp:76) calls memchr for needle[0], then Contains<> calls memchr again for every candidate position. On short strings (about 50 bytes) with common first bytes, that means several libc calls per string, each with setup and branch overhead. A branch-light candidate filter would mostly remove the matcher cost: compare 8 (SWAR) or 16 (SSE2) positions at once against needle[0] at offset i and against needle[n-1] at offset i+n-1, AND the two masks, and verify only the surviving candidates with memcmp (Muła's generic SIMD strstr).
issues.plan: In src/function/scalar/string/contains.cpp, add a fast path inside FindStrInStr(const unsigned char*, idx_t, const unsigned char*, idx_t), used when needle_size >= 2 and haystack_size >= needle_size - 1 + 8. Set first = broadcast(needle[0]) and last = broadcast(needle[n-1]). For i in steps of 8 while i + n - 1 + 8 <= haystack_size: A = Load<uint64_t>(h+i) ^ first; B = Load<uint64_t>(h+i+n-1) ^ last; take the zero-byte mask of (A|B) with the classic haszero ((x - 0x0101..) & ~x & 0x8080..). It can give false positives only above a true zero byte, and memcmp catches those. For each set bit, from low to high: pos = i + ctz(mask)/8; if memcmp(h+pos+1, needle+1, n-2) == 0, return pos (n==2 needs no memcmp). Positions must be visited in ascending order so the leftmost match is returned, because LikeMatcher::Match depends on the leftmost offset. After the loop, hand the remaining tail [i, end) to the existing memchr/Contains<> code with base_offset=i, or to a plain scalar loop. Every load must stay inside [haystack, haystack+haystack_size), with no over-read. Optionally use SSE2 for 16-byte blocks under #ifdef __SSE2__ with _mm_movemask_epi8, keeping the SWAR path as the portable fallback. Little-endian only for ctz bit order: on big-endian, use the existing path (#if on __BYTE_ORDER__). Keep the semantics identical: return the offset of the first match or INVALID_INDEX. Test against the old implementation on random strings, needles of length 1-20, matches at the start, at the end, overlapping and repeated-prefix cases, plus contains/strpos/LIKE/ILIKE queries.
issues.expected_gain: q13: about 0.2-0.35s of the roughly 0.45s matcher CPU (of 3.35s total), so -5 to -10% wall. Any LIKE '%x%', contains, strpos or instr filter on string columns gets faster.
issues.generality: Every substring search: LIKE with % segments, contains(), position/strpos/instr, NOT LIKE, ILIKE after lowercasing if it routes here. No query shape should get slower, except possibly very long haystacks with a rare first byte, where glibc's AVX2 memchr would beat 8-byte SWAR. The SSE2 variant or a fallback to memchr when haystack_size > 256 removes that case.
issues.risk: Low to medium. It is a pure function with exact semantics, but over-reads and returning the leftmost match must be right. It is easy to unit-test against the old code.

issues.title: Remove cancelling decompress/compress projection pair above joins
issues.hypothesis: In the q13 plan, above the RIGHT HASH_JOIN, a PROJECTION applies __internal_decompress_integral_bigint(#1) (0.18s CPU on 15.3M rows, dictionary vectors from the perfect hash join). Right above it, another PROJECTION applies __internal_compress_integral_uinteger(#1) with the same offset for the aggregate's group key. The pair is an identity on the compressed value (the uinteger stays in range, since it was produced by the same compress), so it is wasted work, and it flattens dictionary vectors.
issues.plan: Investigate where compress projections are added (grep for __internal_compress_integral in src/optimizer/compressed_materialization*.cpp). Add a rule that recognises compress_T(decompress_S(x, c), c) with the same constant offset where the compressed type T equals the input type of x, and replace it with x. That holds when the intermediate type is wider and the stats prove the range. Apply it either in CompressedMaterialization or as a peephole when two adjacent projections are merged.
issues.expected_gain: q13: about 0.18s CPU of 3.35s, so -3 to -5%
issues.generality: Any plan where compressed materialization wraps consecutive operators (join then aggregate) on the same integer key.
issues.risk: Medium. The optimizer has to prove the offsets and types match. The gain is near the noise floor alone.
